subject: Physics
title: Laws of Motion
summary: This chapter builds the whole of mechanics on three statements by Newton: a body keeps its state of rest or uniform motion unless a force acts on it, force equals rate of change of momentum, and every force has an equal and opposite reaction. From these you get momentum conservation, equilibrium of a particle, friction, and motion on circular and banked paths.

exam_profile.weightage: Class 11 has no board exam, but this chapter is a major part of the school final (Term/Annual) paper and it is the foundation for Class 12 boards, JEE and NEET — 'Laws of Motion' problems (blocks, pulleys, friction, circular motion) return every year in those papers.

question_types.note: Direction and magnitude of friction, momentum change, reading of a spring balance or weighing machine in a lift, banking angle.
Tests whether you can tell a true statement from its correct explanation, e.g. inertia vs mass, or Newton's third law pairs acting on different bodies.
State a law, define impulse or coefficient of friction, one-line 'why does this happen' questions.
A numerical on F = ma, momentum conservation, or a simple friction/incline problem with full working.
Derive the banking-angle formula, solve a connected-bodies/pulley problem, or derive apparent weight in a lift.
A situational passage — car turning on a road, or a person in a lift — with four sub-questions built on one common force diagram.

hot_topics: Newton's second law, F = ma, and impulse
Conservation of linear momentum (recoil of a gun, explosion, collision)
Newton's third law — identifying action-reaction pairs correctly
Static and kinetic friction, angle of friction, angle of repose
Motion of a car on a level road and on a banked road
Apparent weight in a lift (accelerating up, down, free fall)
Connected bodies and pulley problems (Atwood machine, blocks on a string)
Equilibrium of a particle under concurrent forces

sections.heading: 4.1–4.2 Introduction and Aristotle's Fallacy
sections.body:
Aristotle believed that a force is needed to keep a body moving, and that a moving object comes to rest naturally because that is its 'natural state'. This looks true in daily life — push a book and it stops when you stop pushing — only because friction is quietly acting on the book and slowing it down. Aristotle never separated the effect of friction from the effect of the applied force.

Galileo corrected this with thought experiments on inclined planes. He argued that if a ball rolls down one incline and up another with no friction, it will rise to the same height it started from, however gentle the second slope is made. Push the second slope's angle to zero and the ball would keep moving forever at constant speed, needing no force at all to sustain that motion. Friction and other resistive forces, not motion itself, are what bring bodies to rest — motion needs no cause, only a change in motion does.

This is the seed of the law of inertia: an external force is needed to change a body's state, not to maintain it.
sections.tip: If a question asks 'why did Aristotle's idea seem correct', the answer is always: he did not account for friction and air resistance, not that his logic was internally wrong.

sections.heading: 4.3–4.4 The Law of Inertia and Newton's First Law
sections.body:
Newton's first law: every body continues in its state of rest or of uniform motion in a straight line unless it is compelled to change that state by an external force.

This law does two jobs. First, it defines force qualitatively — force is whatever changes a body's state of rest or uniform velocity. Second, it defines inertia: the natural tendency of a body to resist any change in its state of motion. Inertia is not a force; it is a property, and its measure is mass — the more massive a body, the harder it is to change its velocity.

There are three kinds of inertia, and exam papers like naming them with an everyday example: inertia of rest (a coin on a card flicked off a glass does not move with the card and falls into the glass; passengers jerk backward when a bus starts suddenly), inertia of motion (a passenger standing in a moving bus falls forward when the bus brakes suddenly — the body keeps moving while the feet are stopped by friction), and inertia of direction (mud flies off a spinning cycle tyre tangentially; a stone tied to a string flies off tangentially if the string snaps).

The first law holds only in an inertial frame of reference — one that is at rest or moving with constant velocity. In a frame that itself accelerates (a braking bus, a merry-go-round) objects appear to move without any real force acting on them; that apparent effect is explained using a 'pseudo force', which is not a genuine force and has no reaction pair.
sections.tip: A very common one-mark trap: 'the reason passengers fall forward when a bus stops suddenly' — write it as inertia of motion of the passenger's upper body, not 'force pushes them forward'. There is no forward force; their body simply continues moving.

sections.heading: 4.5 Newton's Second Law of Motion
sections.body:
Momentum p = mv combines the two quantities — mass and velocity — that together decide how hard it is to stop or deflect a moving body. Newton's second law states: the rate of change of momentum of a body is directly proportional to the applied force and takes place in the direction in which the force acts.

Derivation of F = ma. Let a body of mass m move with velocity v under a force F. Its momentum is p = mv. By the second law,

F ∝ dp/dt, so F = k·dp/dt = k·d(mv)/dt.

For a body of constant mass, F = k·m(dv/dt) = k·ma. The unit of force (the newton) is chosen so that a force of 1 N gives a mass of 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m s−2, which fixes k = 1. So F = ma, or more generally F = dp/dt when mass is not constant.

The first law is contained inside the second: if F = 0 then dp/dt = 0, so p (and hence v, for constant mass) stays unchanged — that is exactly the statement of the first law. The second law is a vector law: it applies separately along each of the x, y and z directions, which is why component-wise resolution (Fx = max, etc.) is the standard method for solving inclined-plane and projectile-type force problems.

Impulse. When a large force acts for a very short time (a bat hitting a ball, a collision), it is easier to measure the total effect than the force at each instant. Impulse J = F·Δt = Δp, the change in momentum. This is why cricketers draw their hands back while catching a fast ball, and why vehicles have crumple zones and airbags — increasing Δt for the same Δp reduces the peak force.

where: impulse (N s, same units as momentum)
time for which the force acts

sections.tip: The full derivation F = ma (starting from F ∝ dp/dt) is a very common 2–3 mark question. Always state that k = 1 because of how the newton is defined — examiners look for that line.

sections.heading: 4.6 Newton's Third Law of Motion
sections.body:
Newton's third law: to every action there is an equal and opposite reaction; action and reaction act on two different bodies, never on the same body, and they act simultaneously — neither is 'before' the other.

Because action and reaction act on different bodies, they never cancel each other even though they are equal and opposite; a pair of forces cancels only when both act on the same body. This is the most tested idea from this section: a book resting on a table experiences its weight (from the Earth) and a normal reaction (from the table); these two forces on the book are equal and opposite but they are not an action–reaction pair — they act on the same body and happen to balance by the first law's equilibrium condition, not by the third law. The true third-law partner of the table's normal force on the book is the book pressing down on the table; the true partner of the book's weight is the book pulling the Earth upward with an equal force.

Everyday illustrations examiners like: a swimmer pushes water backward and water pushes the swimmer forward; a gun recoils when a bullet is fired forward; walking is possible because your foot pushes the ground backward and the ground pushes you forward.

where: force on body A due to body B
force on body B due to body A, acting on a different body

sections.tip: Never say 'weight and normal reaction are an action-reaction pair'. Both act on the same object, so by definition they cannot be a third-law pair — this is the single most common mistake in this chapter.

sections.heading: 4.7 Conservation of Linear Momentum
sections.body:
Derivation. Consider two bodies A and B, of masses m1 and m2, colliding for a short time Δt with no external force on the system. Let FAB be the force on A due to B, and FBA the force on B due to A. By Newton's second law,

FAB = (p1f − p1i)/Δt and FBA = (p2f − p2i)/Δt.

By Newton's third law, FAB = −FBA, so (p1f − p1i) = −(p2f − p2i). Rearranging, p1i + p2i = p1f + p2f — the total momentum of an isolated system (no external force) stays constant. This is the law of conservation of linear momentum, and it holds for any number of bodies, colliding, exploding or separating, as long as no external force acts on the system.

The classic application is recoil: a gun and bullet start at rest, so their total initial momentum is zero. When the bullet is fired forward, the gun must recoil backward with exactly enough momentum to keep the total at zero — mbulletvbullet = −mgunvgun. The same idea explains why a rocket accelerates forward by ejecting exhaust gas backward, and why two ice skaters pushing off from each other move apart with momenta equal in magnitude but opposite in direction.

where: initial momenta of the two bodies
final momenta of the two bodies

sections.tip: Always state the condition 'no external force acts on the system' before writing the conservation equation — leaving it out costs a mark in the derivation.

sections.heading: 4.8 Equilibrium of a Particle
sections.body:
A particle is in equilibrium when the vector sum of all forces acting on it is zero: ΣF = 0, which by the second law means its acceleration is zero — it is either at rest or moving with constant velocity.

For two forces, equilibrium needs them equal in magnitude and opposite in direction. For three concurrent forces, equilibrium needs each force to be equal in magnitude to the resultant of the other two but opposite in direction — equivalently, the three force vectors, placed head to tail, must form a closed triangle (this is the triangle law used for equilibrium problems, and it generalises to a closed polygon for more forces). In component form, equilibrium simply requires ΣFx = 0 and ΣFy = 0 separately, which is the practical method used for problems with strings, weights and inclined surfaces.

A weight hanging from two strings attached to a wall or ceiling is the standard equilibrium problem: resolve each string's tension into horizontal and vertical components, set the sum of horizontal components to zero and the sum of vertical components equal to the weight, and solve the two equations together.

where: vector sum of all forces on the particle

sections.tip: Draw a clean free-body diagram before writing any equilibrium equation — most marks lost here are from a missing or wrongly-directed force, not from the algebra.

sections.heading: 4.9 Common Forces in Mechanics
sections.body:
Four forces recur through mechanics: weight (mg, always vertically downward, due to gravity), normal reaction N (perpendicular to the contact surface, a manifestation of the electromagnetic forces between surface atoms resisting inter-penetration), tension T (along a string, pulling inward on whatever it is attached to, same magnitude throughout an ideal massless, inextensible string over a frictionless pulley), and friction f (along the contact surface, opposing relative sliding or its tendency).

Friction is tested the most. Static friction fs is a self-adjusting force that opposes the tendency of relative sliding between surfaces still at rest with respect to each other; it rises to match the applied force up to a maximum value fs,max = μsN, beyond which sliding begins. Kinetic friction fk = μkN acts once sliding has started, and μk is slightly less than μs — this is why it takes a bigger push to start moving a heavy box than to keep it moving. Both laws of friction state that fmax is proportional to the normal reaction N and (to a good approximation) independent of the apparent area of contact.

The angle of friction λ is the angle the resultant of N and fmax makes with N; tan λ = μs. The angle of repose θ is the angle of an incline at which a body just begins to slide under gravity alone; at that angle mg sin θ = fs,max = μsmg cos θ, so tan θ = μs — numerically the angle of repose equals the angle of friction.

Friction is not always unwanted: walking, writing and the grip of tyres on a road all depend on it. Where it is unwanted (machine bearings), it is reduced by lubrication or by replacing sliding friction with rolling friction, which is much smaller because rolling contact deforms the surfaces far less than sliding contact.

where: coefficient of kinetic friction, μ<sub>k</sub> < μ<sub>s</sub>
incline angle at which sliding just begins

sections.tip: Static friction is not always at its maximum value — it equals whatever is needed to prevent sliding, up to μsN. A very common wrong step is writing f = μsN for a body that is not on the verge of sliding.

sections.heading: 4.10 Circular Motion — Car on a Level Road and on a Banked Road
sections.body:
A car going around a circular path needs a centripetal force mv²/r directed toward the centre. On a level (unbanked) road, only friction between the tyres and the road can supply this force, so mv²/r ≤ μsmg, giving a maximum safe speed vmax = √(μsrg). Beyond this speed the car skids outward.

Banked road (no friction) — derivation. Bank the road at angle θ to the horizontal. The two forces on the car are its weight mg (down) and the normal reaction N (perpendicular to the road surface, so tilted at θ to the vertical). Resolving N into components: N cos θ balances the weight, and N sin θ supplies the centripetal force.

N cos θ = mg …(i)
N sin θ = mv²/r …(ii)

Dividing (ii) by (i): tan θ = v²/(rg), so the optimum (safe, no-friction-needed) speed is v = √(rg tan θ). At this exact speed, friction is not needed at all; below it the car tends to slide down the slope (friction must act up the slope), above it the car tends to skid outward up the slope (friction must act down the slope).

Banked road with friction. Including the maximum static friction μsN acting down the slope (to prevent outward skidding at high speed) gives the maximum speed:

vmax = √[rg(μs + tan θ)/(1 − μstan θ)].

Banking is used on real roads and railway tracks so that a safe range of speeds is possible with less dependence on friction, which reduces tyre wear and the risk of skidding, especially on a wet road where μs drops sharply.

where: maximum safe speed on a level road
coefficient of static friction between tyre and banked road

sections.tip: The banked-road derivation (tan θ = v²/rg) is one of the most repeated 3–5 mark derivations from this chapter across boards, JEE and NEET — practise it until you can reproduce the two resolved equations without hesitation.

sections.heading: 4.11 Solving Problems in Mechanics — Connected Bodies, Pulleys, Apparent Weight
sections.body:
A fixed method solves almost every problem in this chapter: draw a free-body diagram for each body separately, mark every real force (never a fictitious one, unless you have deliberately chosen a non-inertial frame), choose a positive direction along the expected motion, and apply Fnet = ma along that direction for each body. Then combine the equations.

Two blocks connected by a string over a pulley (Atwood machine), hanging on either side. For masses m1 and m2 (m2 > m1) connected by a light, inextensible string over a frictionless, massless pulley: taking the direction of actual motion as positive for each mass,

m2g − T = m2a and T − m1g = m1a.

Adding the two equations eliminates T: a = (m2 − m1)g/(m1 + m2), and substituting back gives T = m1m2(1 + g/... simplified as T = m1(g + a) = 2m1m2g/(m1 + m2).

Apparent weight in a lift. A person of mass m stands on a weighing machine inside a lift; the machine reads the normal reaction N it exerts on the person, which by the third law equals the force the person exerts on it. Applying F = ma to the person (taking upward as positive when the lift accelerates upward with acceleration a): N − mg = ma, so N = m(g + a) — the person feels heavier. If the lift accelerates downward, N = m(g − a) — the person feels lighter. If the lift falls freely (a = g, cable snapped), N = 0 — apparent weightlessness, even though gravity is still fully acting.

The same free-body method extends to blocks on inclined planes (resolve mg into mg sin θ along the slope and mg cos θ perpendicular to it) and to blocks connected on a table with a hanging mass over a pulley at the edge.

where: the two masses of an Atwood machine

formulas.expr: N = m(g ± a); N = 0 in free fall

sections.tip: In lift problems, always define 'a' as the lift's acceleration and check its sign against the direction of acceleration stated in the question before plugging into N = m(g ± a) — sign errors here are the single biggest cause of lost marks.

key_terms.definition: The inherent property of a body by virtue of which it resists any change in its state of rest or of uniform motion; its measure is mass.
A frame of reference that is at rest or moving with constant velocity, in which Newton's first law holds without needing a pseudo force.
The product of a body's mass and velocity, p = mv; a vector quantity in the direction of velocity.
The product of a large force and the short time for which it acts, equal to the change in momentum it produces: J = FΔt = Δp.
The rate of change of momentum of a body is directly proportional to the applied force and takes place in the direction of the force; leads to F = ma.
To every action there is an equal and opposite reaction; action and reaction act simultaneously on two different bodies.

key_terms.term: Law of conservation of linear momentum
key_terms.definition: The total momentum of an isolated system of bodies (no external force) remains constant, however the bodies interact within the system.
The state of a particle when the vector sum of all forces acting on it is zero, so its acceleration is zero.
The contact force a surface exerts on a body, perpendicular to the surface, that prevents the body from penetrating it.
The pulling force transmitted through a stretched string or cable, directed along the string, equal throughout an ideal massless string.
The self-adjusting opposing force between two surfaces at relative rest, equal to the applied force up to a maximum value μsN.
The opposing force between two surfaces in relative sliding motion, of constant value μkN, acting opposite to the relative velocity.
The ratio of the limiting frictional force to the normal reaction between two surfaces; a property of the pair of surfaces in contact, roughly independent of contact area.
The maximum angle of inclination of a surface at which a body placed on it just remains on the verge of sliding under gravity alone; tan θ = μs.

The net force directed toward the centre of a circular path that is required to keep a body moving on that circular path; not a new kind of force but the resultant of real forces (friction, tension, normal reaction, etc.).

The angle at which the outer edge of a curved road or track is raised above the inner edge, so that part of the normal reaction supplies the centripetal force needed for circular motion, reducing dependence on friction.
A fictitious force introduced in a non-inertial (accelerating) frame of reference to make Newton's second law appear to hold there; it has no reaction pair and no real physical origin.
The reading shown by a weighing scale under a body, equal to the normal reaction the scale exerts on the body; differs from true weight mg whenever the body has vertical acceleration.

formula_sheet.name: Newton's second law
formula_sheet.note: for constant mass; vector equation, apply component-wise

formula_sheet.name: Impulse–momentum theorem
formula_sheet.note: used for short-duration large forces (collisions, impacts)

formula_sheet.name: Conservation of momentum
formula_sheet.note: valid only when no external force acts on the system

formula_sheet.name: Limiting static friction
formula_sheet.note: maximum value static friction can take before sliding starts

formula_sheet.name: Kinetic friction
formula_sheet.note: constant while sliding continues; μ<sub>k</sub> < μ<sub>s</sub>

formula_sheet.name: Angle of repose / angle of friction
formula_sheet.note: incline angle at which a body just starts to slide

formula_sheet.name: Max speed on level circular road
formula_sheet.note: centripetal force supplied entirely by friction

formula_sheet.name: Optimum speed on banked road (frictionless)
formula_sheet.note: no tendency to skid up or slide down at this speed

formula_sheet.name: Max speed on banked road (with friction)
formula_sheet.note: friction acts down the slope to prevent outward skidding

formula_sheet.name: Acceleration of an Atwood machine
formula_sheet.note: two masses over a frictionless, massless pulley, m<sub>2</sub> > m<sub>1</sub>

formula_sheet.name: Apparent weight in a lift
formula_sheet.expr: N = m(g + a) accelerating up; N = m(g − a) accelerating down; N = 0 in free fall
formula_sheet.note: a is the lift's acceleration magnitude

diagrams.title: Free-body diagram of a block on a rough inclined plane
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw the incline at angle θ with a block on it. From the block's centre, draw four arrows: mg vertically down, resolved into mg sin θ along the slope (down the incline) and mg cos θ perpendicular into the slope (dashed construction lines for the resolution); N perpendicular to the incline surface, out of it; f along the incline, pointing up the slope (opposing the tendency to slide down) if the block is about to slide down, or down the slope if being pushed up. Label θ at the base and show the resolution triangle clearly — examiners award marks for the resolution being shown, not just the final forces.

diagrams.title: Car on a banked road — force diagram for the banking derivation
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw the cross-section of the road banked at angle θ to the horizontal, with the car (a small box) on the slope, centre of the circular path to the left at distance r. Draw N perpendicular to the road surface (tilted at θ from the vertical) and mg vertically downward from the car. Drop a dashed vertical line and dashed horizontal line from the tip of N to show its components N cos θ (vertical, balancing mg) and N sin θ (horizontal, pointing toward the centre, supplying mv²/r). Mark θ between N and the vertical construction line.

diagrams.title: Atwood machine (two masses over a pulley)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw a fixed frictionless pulley at the top with a string over it; hang mass m<sub>1</sub> on the left and the heavier mass m<sub>2</sub> on the right. Draw T pointing upward (toward the pulley) on both masses, equal in length on each side since the string is ideal. Draw m<sub>1</sub>g downward on the left mass and m<sub>2</sub>g downward on the right mass. Show the direction of acceleration a with an arrow: downward for m<sub>2</sub>, upward for m<sub>1</sub>, since m<sub>2</sub> > m<sub>1</sub>.

diagrams.title: Apparent weight in an accelerating lift
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw a person standing on a weighing machine inside a lift cabin. Draw two forces on the person only: mg downward (true weight) and N upward (normal reaction from the machine, equal to the machine's reading). Draw an arrow beside the lift showing its acceleration a — label it 'upward' for one case and 'downward' for another, and note beside each case whether N is greater or less than mg.

ncert_questions.q: A force of 5 N gives a mass m<sub>1</sub> an acceleration of 8 m s<sup>−2</sup> and a mass m<sub>2</sub> an acceleration of 24 m s<sup>−2</sup>. What acceleration would the same force give if both masses were tied together?

A bullet of mass 0.04 kg moving with a speed of 90 m s<sup>−1</sup> enters a heavy wooden block and is stopped after a distance of 60 cm. What is the average resistive force exerted by the block on the bullet?
ncert_questions.a:
Using v² = u² − 2as with v = 0, u = 90 m s−1, s = 0.6 m:

0 = 90² − 2a(0.6) ⇒ a = 8100/1.2 = 6750 m s−2 (deceleration).

F = ma = 0.04 × 6750 = 270 N, directed opposite to the bullet's motion.

ncert_questions.q: A shell of mass 0.020 kg is fired by a gun of mass 100 kg. If the muzzle speed of the shell is 80 m s<sup>−1</sup>, what is the recoil speed of the gun?
ncert_questions.a:
By conservation of momentum, taking the system initially at rest:

mgunvgun = mshellvshell

vgun = (0.020 × 80)/100 = 1.6/100 = 0.016 m s−1, directed opposite to the shell's motion.

ncert_questions.q: State Newton's second law of motion and use it to derive the equation F = ma for a body of constant mass.
ncert_questions.a:
Newton's second law: the rate of change of momentum of a body is directly proportional to the applied force and takes place in the direction of the force.

F ∝ dp/dt ⇒ F = k·d(mv)/dt. For constant mass, F = k·m(dv/dt) = kma. The newton is defined so that 1 N gives 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m s−2, which fixes k = 1. Hence F = ma.

ncert_questions.q: Two billiard balls, each of mass 0.05 kg, moving in opposite directions with speed 6 m s<sup>−1</sup> each, collide and rebound with the same speed. What is the impulse imparted to each ball by the other?
ncert_questions.a:
Take the direction of the first ball's initial motion as positive. Initial momentum of ball A = 0.05 × 6 = 0.3 kg m s−1; after rebound its momentum is −0.3 kg m s−1.

Impulse on A = Δp = (−0.3) − (0.3) = −0.6 kg m s−1 (magnitude 0.6 N s, opposite to its initial direction).

By Newton's third law, the impulse on ball B is +0.6 kg m s−1, equal and opposite.

ncert_questions.q: Derive an expression for the maximum speed with which a car can go round a level curved road of radius r without skidding, given the coefficient of static friction μs between the tyres and the road.
ncert_questions.a:
On a level road only friction supplies the centripetal force needed: f = mv²/r. The maximum available friction is fmax = μsN = μsmg (since N = mg on a level road).

For no skidding, mv²/r ≤ μsmg, so v² ≤ μsrg, giving vmax = √(μsrg).

ncert_questions.q: A block of mass 4 kg is resting on a horizontal surface. If the coefficient of static friction between the block and surface is 0.5, find the minimum horizontal force needed to just move the block. (Take g = 9.8 m s<sup>−2</sup>.)
ncert_questions.a:
Normal reaction N = mg = 4 × 9.8 = 39.2 N.

Maximum static friction fs,max = μsN = 0.5 × 39.2 = 19.6 N. This is the minimum force needed to just start the block moving.

ncert_questions.q: Two masses of 4 kg and 6 kg are connected by a light, inextensible string passing over a frictionless pulley fixed at the edge of a table, with the 6 kg mass hanging freely (Atwood-type arrangement, both hanging on either side). Find the acceleration of the system and the tension in the string. (g = 9.8 m s<sup>−2</sup>)
ncert_questions.a:
For m2 = 6 kg (moving down): m2g − T = m2a.

For m1 = 4 kg (moving up): T − m1g = m1a.

Adding: (m2 − m1)g = (m1 + m2)a ⇒ a = (6 − 4)(9.8)/10 = 1.96 m s−2.

T = m1(g + a) = 4(9.8 + 1.96) = 4 × 11.76 = 47.04 N.

ncert_questions.q: A man of mass 70 kg stands on a weighing machine in a lift which is moving upward with an acceleration of 1.2 m s<sup>−2</sup>. What is the reading of the weighing machine? (g = 9.8 m s<sup>−2</sup>)
ncert_questions.a: For upward acceleration, apparent weight N = m(g + a) = 70(9.8 + 1.2) = 70 × 11.0 = 770 N, which the machine reads as a mass of 770/9.8 ≈ 78.6 kg.

ncert_questions.q: A cyclist speeding at 18 km h<sup>−1</sup> on a level road takes a sharp circular turn of radius 3 m without reducing speed. The coefficient of static friction between the tyres and the road is 0.1. Will the cyclist slip while taking the turn?
ncert_questions.a:
v = 18 km h−1 = 5 m s−1. Required centripetal acceleration = v²/r = 25/3 ≈ 8.33 m s−2.

Maximum acceleration frictioncan provide = μsg = 0.1 × 9.8 = 0.98 m s−2.

Since the required acceleration (8.33 m s−2) far exceeds what friction can supply (0.98 m s−2), the cyclist will skid while taking the turn at this speed.

ncert_questions.q: A road is banked at an angle of 30° for negotiating a curve of radius 100 m. At what speed should a car travel round the curve so that it does not slip and friction is not needed? (g = 9.8 m s<sup>−2</sup>, tan 30° ≈ 0.577)

pyq.q: A body of mass 2 kg is moving with a constant velocity of 5 m s<sup>−1</sup> on a smooth horizontal surface. The net force acting on the body is:
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: Constant velocity means zero acceleration; by F = ma, the net force must be zero.

pyq.q: When a bus suddenly starts moving forward, the passengers standing in it tend to fall backward. This is due to:
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: The passengers' feet move with the bus but their upper body tends to stay at rest — inertia of rest.

pyq.q: The coefficient of kinetic friction between two surfaces is generally:
options: Greater than the coefficient of static friction
Equal to the coefficient of static friction
Less than the coefficient of static friction
Independent of the coefficient of static friction
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: Once sliding begins, less force is needed to sustain it than to start it, so μk < μs.

pyq.q: A man in a lift feels his apparent weight to be zero. The lift must be:
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: N = m(g − a); N = 0 only when a = g, i.e. the lift (and the man) are in free fall.

pyq.q: A gun of mass 5 kg fires a bullet of mass 50 g with a muzzle velocity of 200 m s<sup>−1</sup>. The recoil velocity of the gun is:
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: By momentum conservation, v_gun = (0.05 × 200)/5 = 10/5 = 2 m s⁻¹.

pyq.q: Which of the following pairs of forces is a correct example of a Newton's third law action–reaction pair?
options: Weight of a book and the normal reaction of the table on the book
The push of a swimmer's hand on water and the push of water on the swimmer
Tension in a string and the weight of the block it supports
Gravitational force on a ball and air resistance on the ball
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: Action–reaction pairs act on two different bodies (swimmer and water); the other options list two forces on the same body.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): Mass and inertia of a body are the same physical quantity. Reason (R): A body with greater mass has a greater tendency to resist a change in its state of rest or motion.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: d
pyq.solution: Mass is the measure of inertia, not identical to it as a concept; R correctly describes inertia, so A is false and R is true.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): A car can be driven faster round a banked curve than round a similar unbanked curve of the same radius. Reason (R): On a banked road, part of the normal reaction contributes to the centripetal force, reducing the dependence on friction.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: Banking lets N sin θ supply part or all of the centripetal force, allowing a higher safe speed than friction alone provides on a level road; R correctly explains A.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): When a body is in equilibrium under three concurrent forces, the forces can be represented by the three sides of a triangle taken in order. Reason (R): The equilibrium of a particle requires that the vector sum of all forces acting on it be zero.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: Zero vector sum for three vectors is geometrically the condition for a closed triangle when the vectors are placed head to tail; R correctly explains A.

pyq.q: Why is it easier to pull a lawn roller than to push it, for the same magnitude of applied force?
pyq.answer: When pulling, the applied force is directed upward at an angle to the horizontal, so its vertical component reduces the effective normal reaction (N = mg − F sin θ), which lowers the friction (f = μN) opposing motion. When pushing, the vertical component of the force adds to the weight, increasing N (N = mg + F sin θ) and hence friction. So for the same applied force, pulling needs less effort to overcome friction than pushing.

pyq.q: A stone of mass 0.1 kg tied to the end of a string of length 1 m is whirled in a horizontal circle at a constant speed of 4 m s<sup>−1</sup>. What is the tension in the string providing the centripetal force?
pyq.answer: T = mv²/r = 0.1 × 4²/1 = 0.1 × 16 = 1.6 N, directed along the string toward the centre of the circle.

pyq.q: State the law of conservation of linear momentum and mention the condition under which it holds.
pyq.answer: The total linear momentum of an isolated system of interacting bodies remains constant, provided no external force acts on the system. It follows directly from Newton's second and third laws — the internal forces bodies in the system exert on each other occur in equal and opposite pairs, so they cannot change the total momentum of the system, only redistribute it among the bodies.

pyq.q: Define angle of repose. How is it related to the coefficient of static friction?
pyq.answer: The angle of repose is the maximum angle of inclination of a rough surface at which a body placed on it just remains on the verge of sliding down under its own weight, without any external push. At this angle, tan θ = μs, the coefficient of static friction between the body and the surface — the angle of repose is numerically equal to the angle of friction.

pyq.q: A block of mass 5 kg is placed on a rough horizontal surface with coefficient of kinetic friction 0.2. A horizontal force of 20 N is applied to it. Find the acceleration of the block. (g = 9.8 m s<sup>−2</sup>)
pyq.answer:
Normal reaction N = mg = 5 × 9.8 = 49 N.

Kinetic friction fk = μkN = 0.2 × 49 = 9.8 N, opposing motion.

Net force = 20 − 9.8 = 10.2 N.

a = Fnet/m = 10.2/5 = 2.04 m s−2.

pyq.q: Two masses of 8 kg and 12 kg are connected at the two ends of a light, inextensible string that passes over a frictionless pulley. Find the acceleration of the masses and the tension in the string when the masses are released from rest. (g = 9.8 m s<sup>−2</sup>)
Explain, with a labelled force diagram, why a passenger standing in a bus tends to fall forward when the bus applies sudden brakes.
pyq.answer: Before braking, both the bus and the standing passenger move with the same velocity. When the brakes are applied, friction from the road decelerates the bus (and the passenger's feet, which are in contact with the floor through friction) suddenly. The upper part of the passenger's body, having no direct force acting to slow it down, tends by inertia of motion to continue moving forward at the original speed while the feet have already slowed down — so the body pitches forward relative to the bus. (Diagram: passenger's feet shown with a backward friction arrow near the floor; upper body shown continuing forward with a dashed 'original velocity' arrow.)

pyq.q: A ball of mass 0.15 kg moving with a speed of 12 m s<sup>−1</sup> strikes a wall normally and rebounds with the same speed. If the time of contact with the wall is 0.01 s, calculate the average force exerted by the ball on the wall.
pyq.answer:
Taking the initial direction of the ball as positive: initial momentum = 0.15 × 12 = 1.8 kg m s−1; final momentum = −1.8 kg m s−1 (rebound).

Δp = −1.8 − 1.8 = −3.6 kg m s−1.

Force on the ball = Δp/Δt = −3.6/0.01 = −360 N, i.e. 360 N directed away from the wall on the ball.

By Newton's third law, the ball exerts a force of 360 N on the wall, directed into the wall.

pyq.q: Derive an expression for the maximum speed with which a car can safely negotiate a curved road of radius r, banked at angle θ, given the coefficient of static friction μs between the tyres and the road.
pyq.answer:
On a banked road with friction, at maximum speed the car is on the verge of skidding outward up the slope, so friction f = μsN acts down the slope, toward the centre's side of the incline.

Resolving forces along the vertical: N cos θ = mg + f sin θ = mg + μsN sin θ, so N(cos θ − μssin θ) = mg …(i)

Resolving along the horizontal (toward the centre): N sin θ + f cos θ = mv²max/r, so N(sin θ + μscos θ) = mv²max/r …(ii)

Dividing (ii) by (i): v²max/(rg) = (sin θ + μscos θ)/(cos θ − μssin θ). Dividing numerator and denominator by cos θ:

v²max = rg(tan θ + μs)/(1 − μstan θ), so vmax = √[rg(μs + tan θ)/(1 − μstan θ)]. When μs = 0, this reduces to the frictionless result v = √(rg tan θ).

pyq.q: State Newton's three laws of motion. Using the second and third laws, derive the law of conservation of linear momentum for a two-body collision with no external force.
pyq.answer:
First law: A body continues in its state of rest or uniform motion in a straight line unless acted on by an external force. Second law: The rate of change of momentum of a body is proportional to the applied force and takes place in the direction of the force, F = dp/dt. Third law: To every action there is an equal and opposite reaction, acting on two different bodies simultaneously.

Derivation: Let bodies A (mass m1) and B (mass m2) collide for time Δt, with no external force on the pair. Let FAB be the force on A due to B, and FBA the force on B due to A. By the second law, FAB = (p1f − p1i)/Δt and FBA = (p2f − p2i)/Δt. By the third law, FAB = −FBA. So (p1f − p1i)/Δt = −(p2f − p2i)/Δt, giving p1f + p2f = p1i + p2i — total momentum before equals total momentum after, i.e. momentum is conserved for the isolated pair.

pyq.q: A block of mass 10 kg is placed on a rough inclined plane of angle 30° with the horizontal. The coefficient of static friction between the block and the incline is 0.3. (a) Show, with calculation, whether the block remains at rest or slides down. (b) If it slides, find its acceleration. (g = 9.8 m s<sup>−2</sup>, sin 30° = 0.5, cos 30° = 0.866)
pyq.answer:
Component of weight along the incline (driving force) = mg sin 30° = 10 × 9.8 × 0.5 = 49 N.

Normal reaction N = mg cos 30° = 10 × 9.8 × 0.866 = 84.87 N.

Maximum available static friction = μsN = 0.3 × 84.87 = 25.46 N.

(a) Since the driving force (49 N) exceeds the maximum static friction (25.46 N), the block slides down the incline.

(b) Once sliding, kinetic friction (taking μk ≈ μs = 0.3 here) = 25.46 N acts up the incline. Net force down the incline = 49 − 25.46 = 23.54 N. Acceleration a = 23.54/10 = 2.35 m s−2, down the incline.

pyq.q:
A racing car of mass 800 kg is moving on a circular banked track of radius 120 m, banked at 15° to the horizontal. Assume the road-tyre coefficient of static friction is 0.35, and g = 9.8 m s−2, tan 15° ≈ 0.268.
(i) What is the optimum speed at which the car needs no friction to go round the track?
(ii) Why is banking preferred over relying only on friction on a level road?
(iii) What provides the centripetal force on the car when it moves exactly at the optimum speed?
(iv) If the car's actual speed is higher than the optimum speed found in (i), in which direction does friction act, and why?
pyq.answer:
(i) v = √(rg tan θ) = √(120 × 9.8 × 0.268) = √315.17 ≈ 17.75 m s−1 (about 63.9 km h−1).

(ii) Banking lets a component of the normal reaction (N sin θ) supply part of the centripetal force, so the car does not have to depend entirely on friction, which can fail on a wet or worn road; this allows a higher safe range of speeds and less tyre wear.

(iii) At exactly the optimum speed, the horizontal component of the normal reaction alone (N sin θ) supplies the full centripetal force; friction is zero.

(iv) Above the optimum speed the car tends to skid outward and up the slope, so friction acts down the slope (toward the centre's side) to help supply the extra centripetal force needed.

pyq.q:
Ravi (mass 60 kg) is standing on a weighing machine inside a lift. Take g = 9.8 m s−2.
(i) The lift starts moving upward with an acceleration of 2 m s−2. What does the weighing machine read?
(ii) The lift then moves up at a constant velocity of 3 m s−1. What does the machine read now?
(iii) The lift then decelerates at 2 m s−2 while still moving upward, just before stopping. What does the machine read?
(iv) If the lift cable were to snap and the lift fell freely, what would the machine read, and why?
pyq.answer:
(i) N = m(g + a) = 60(9.8 + 2) = 60 × 11.8 = 708 N.

(ii) At constant velocity, acceleration = 0, so N = mg = 60 × 9.8 = 588 N, the true weight.

(iii) Decelerating while moving up means the acceleration points downward, so N = m(g − a) = 60(9.8 − 2) = 60 × 7.8 = 468 N.

(iv) In free fall, a = g, so N = m(g − g) = 0 N — the machine would read zero because both Ravi and the lift floor accelerate downward at the same rate g, so there is no relative push between his feet and the floor.

practice_mcq.q: A body will continue moving with uniform velocity unless it is acted upon by:
practice_mcq.explanation: Newton's first law: only a net (unbalanced) external force can change a body's state of uniform velocity.

practice_mcq.q: The SI unit of impulse is the same as the SI unit of:
practice_mcq.explanation: Impulse equals change in momentum, so both are measured in kg m s⁻¹ (equivalently N s).

practice_mcq.q: A 2 kg body is acted upon by a force that changes its velocity from 3 m s⁻¹ to 7 m s⁻¹ in 2 s. The magnitude of the force is:
Which statement about action and reaction forces (Newton's third law) is correct?
options: They act on the same body and cancel out
They act on two different bodies and never cancel out
The action always occurs before the reaction
They are unequal because one body is usually heavier
practice_mcq.explanation: Action and reaction act simultaneously on two different bodies, so they can never cancel each other.

options: It pushes against the air below it
Of the reaction to the backward ejection of exhaust gases, by momentum conservation
Gravity temporarily reverses near the rocket
The fuel becomes lighter than air
practice_mcq.explanation: The rocket and expelled gas form an isolated system; ejecting gas backward gives the rocket forward momentum, working even in vacuum.

practice_mcq.q: Two bodies of masses 3 kg and 5 kg are moving with velocities 2 m s⁻¹ and −2 m s⁻¹ respectively (opposite directions) and stick together after collision. Their common velocity after collision is:
options: 0.5 m s⁻¹ in the direction of the 3 kg body
0.5 m s⁻¹ in the direction of the 5 kg body
1 m s⁻¹ in the direction of the 3 kg body
practice_mcq.explanation: Total momentum = 3(2) + 5(−2) = 6 − 10 = −4 kg m s⁻¹; v = −4/8 = −0.5 m s⁻¹, i.e. 0.5 m s⁻¹ in the direction the 5 kg body was moving.

practice_mcq.q: The normal reaction between a book and a horizontal table on which it rests, and the weight of the book, are:
options: An action–reaction pair by Newton's third law
Equal and opposite because the book is in equilibrium, but not a third-law pair
practice_mcq.explanation: They act on the same body (the book) and happen to balance by the first law's equilibrium condition; a genuine third-law pair must act on two different bodies.

practice_mcq.q: A block placed on a rough surface just begins to slide when the incline is tilted to 37°. The coefficient of static friction between block and surface is approximately (tan 37° ≈ 0.75):
practice_mcq.explanation: At the angle of repose, tan θ = μs, so μs = tan 37° ≈ 0.75.

practice_mcq.q: Rolling friction is much smaller than sliding friction mainly because:
options: The contact area during rolling produces far less surface deformation than sliding contact
Rolling friction does not depend on the normal reaction
There is no contact at all during rolling
practice_mcq.explanation: Sliding drags and deforms surface irregularities much more than rolling contact does, so rolling friction is much smaller for the same normal load.

practice_mcq.q: A car of mass 1000 kg moves on a level circular road of radius 50 m. If μs between tyres and road is 0.4, the maximum speed at which it can turn without skidding is (g = 9.8 m s⁻²):
On a road banked at angle θ, at the optimum speed v = √(rg tan θ), the frictional force required is:
practice_mcq.explanation: At the optimum speed the horizontal component of N alone provides the exact centripetal force needed, so no friction is required.

practice_mcq.q: A person of mass 50 kg stands in a lift accelerating downward at 4.9 m s⁻² (half of g). The reading of a weighing scale under his feet is approximately (g = 9.8 m s⁻²):
In an Atwood machine with masses 3 kg and 5 kg over a frictionless pulley, the tension in the string is (g = 9.8 m s⁻²):
Three forces of equal magnitude act on a particle such that it is in equilibrium. The angle between any two of these forces must be:
practice_mcq.explanation: For three equal forces to sum to zero, they must be arranged symmetrically at 120° to each other, forming an equilateral triangle when placed head to tail.

practice_mcq.q: A pseudo force is introduced when analysing motion in:
practice_mcq.explanation: Pseudo forces are needed only to make Newton's second law appear to hold in an accelerating (non-inertial) frame; they have no real reaction pair.

common_mistakes: Calling the weight of a body and the normal reaction on it a Newton's third-law pair — they act on the same body, so they cannot be an action–reaction pair; the true pairs act on two different objects.

Writing static friction as always equal to μsN — static friction only reaches this maximum value when the body is on the verge of sliding; otherwise it equals whatever is needed to keep the body at rest.

Forgetting to check the sign of acceleration in lift problems, leading to N = m(g + a) being used when the lift is actually decelerating or moving down, giving a wrongly larger 'apparent weight' than the correct value.

Treating centripetal force as a separate, new type of force — it is only the name for the net inward force, which must be identified as friction, tension, or a component of the normal reaction depending on the situation.

Skipping the free-body diagram and writing equations directly — this is where sign errors and missing forces (like forgetting friction, or forgetting a component of tension) creep in and lose marks even when the final formula is remembered correctly.

Confusing mass and inertia as if they were the same word for the same thing, when inertia is the property and mass is its numerical measure — examiners test this distinction directly in Assertion–Reason questions.

In the banked-road derivation, resolving N cos θ and N sin θ the wrong way round (swapping which one balances gravity and which one gives the centripetal component) because the angle θ was measured from the wrong reference line.
strategy:
This chapter rewards derivation practice more than memorisation. Get comfortable writing the F = ma derivation from F ∝ dp/dt, the momentum-conservation proof from the second and third laws together, and the full banked-road derivation (both with and without friction) without looking anything up — these three derivations, in some form, appear across boards, JEE and NEET every year.

For numericals, master one method — draw the free-body diagram, resolve forces along and perpendicular to the direction of motion, apply Fnet = ma — and use it identically for every problem type: blocks on a table, blocks on an incline, connected bodies over a pulley, and a person in a lift. Once this method is automatic, the 'context' of the question (a car, a lift, a string) stops mattering; only the forces in the diagram matter.

Keep a short list of everyday examples for each idea (inertia of rest/motion/direction, action-reaction pairs, why banking helps) — a large share of the one- and two-mark questions simply ask you to identify or explain a familiar situation using the correct law, and a ready example saves time under exam pressure.

Spend the last day before the exam only on: the three laws in exact words, the four common forces and their directions, the friction formulas, and re-deriving the banked-road and Atwood-machine results from scratch, twice each.
revision_checklist: Can state Newton's first, second and third laws in the exact NCERT wording
Can explain why Aristotle's idea seemed true (friction was not accounted for)
Can name and give an everyday example of inertia of rest, motion and direction
Can derive F = ma from F ∝ dp/dt, including why k = 1
Can define impulse and use J = FΔt = Δp in a numerical
Can explain why weight and normal reaction on the same body are NOT a third-law pair
Can derive the law of conservation of momentum from Newton's second and third laws
Can solve a recoil/explosion momentum problem (gun-bullet, two-body separation)
Can state the equilibrium condition for a particle and apply ΣFx = 0, ΣFy = 0
Knows the difference between static and kinetic friction and that μk < μs
Can define angle of repose and connect it to tan θ = μs
Can derive v = √(rg tan θ) for a frictionless banked road, and the version with friction
Can solve an Atwood-machine (connected masses over a pulley) problem for a and T
Can derive apparent weight N = m(g ± a) for a lift and identify the free-fall (N = 0) case
Can draw a correct, fully-labelled free-body diagram for a block on an incline
